In Cartesian coordinates, write ∂i​=∂/∂xi​ and use the Levi-Civita symbol. The contraction of two Levi-Civita symbols gives
[∇×(∇×A)]i​​=ϵijk​ϵklm​∂j​∂l​Am​=(δil​δjm​−δim​δjl​)∂j​∂l​Am​=∂i​∂j​Aj​−∂j​∂j​Ai​.​
(1)
Here the Kronecker delta selects the indicated indices, and continuous second partial derivatives allow their order to be interchanged. Identifying the gradient, divergence and componentwise Laplacian proves the curl of the curl identity:
∇×(∇×A)=∇(∇⋅A)−∇2A.​
(2)

Let V⊂R3 be a bounded region with piecewise smooth closed boundary ∂V, let n be its outward unit normal vector, and let A be a continuously differentiable vector field on a neighbourhood of its closure. The divergence theorem states
∫V​∇⋅AdV=∫∂V​A⋅ndS.​
(3)
Here dV is the positive volume measure, dS is the surface area measure, ∇⋅A=∂x​Ax​+∂y​Ay​+∂z​Az​, and the right side is the total outward flux. All boundary components must be included, with their normals pointing away from V.

Solution

Words: 123
c OurBigBook.com
Differentiate the position vector with respect to the three coordinates:
rρ​ru​rv​​=(sinhρcosucosv,sinhρcosusinv,coshρsinu),=(−coshρsinucosv,−coshρsinusinv,sinhρcosu),=(−coshρcosusinv,coshρcosucosv,0).​
(4)
Their pairwise dot products vanish. For example, rρ​⋅ru​=−sinhρcoshρsinucosu+sinhρcoshρsinucosu=0. Thus these are orthogonal coordinates wherever the coordinate tangents are nonzero. Their scale factors of orthogonal coordinates are
hρ2​=hu2​=sinh2ρcos2u+cosh2ρsin2u=sinh2ρ+sin2u,hv​=coshρcosu.
(5)
The absolute Jacobian determinant is their product, giving
dV=coshρcosu(sinh2ρ+sin2u)dρdudv.​
(6)
The ordered coordinate system is left handed: rρ​⋅(ru​×rv​)=−hρ​hu​hv​. The volume measure uses the absolute value. The axis and the focal circle contain coordinate degeneracies, as expected for oblate spheroidal coordinates. This is the hyperbolic parametrization of oblate spheroidal coordinates. The local TeX has an OCR substitution sinh2u in the volume formula; the original PDF correctly prints sin2u.

Solution

Words: 137
d OurBigBook.com
Put s2=x2+y2. For ρ>0, elimination of u gives
cosh2ρs2​+sinh2ρz2​=1.​
(7)
These are oblate spheroids with equatorial radius coshρ and polar radius sinhρ, flattened along the z axis. At ρ=0 the limiting surface is the disk z=0, s≤1.
For 0<∣u∣<π/2, elimination of ρ instead gives
cos2us2​−sin2uz2​=1.​
(8)
These are one-sheet hyperboloids of revolution, restricted to their upper half for u>0 and lower half for u<0. The restriction matters because ρ≥0. At u=0, the surface degenerates to the exterior equatorial plane z=0, s≥1; at u=±π/2 it degenerates to the corresponding half of the z axis.
Finally, fixed v specifies a vertical half-plane through the z axis, with horizontal direction (cosv,sinv). The two values v and v+π together give a full plane. These surfaces form the mutually orthogonal families of the hyperbolic parametrization of oblate spheroidal coordinates.

For a nondegenerate surface take R>0, and abbreviate C=coshR, H=sinhR. Close the upper oblate spheroid by its equatorial disk D, obtaining a half-ellipsoid V. The divergence is
∇⋅A=y2+2y.
(9)
The integral of 2y vanishes by reflection symmetry. At height z, the cross-section is a disk of radius q=C1−z2/H2​. Using planar polar coordinates,
∫x2+y2≤q2​y2dxdy=∫02π​sin2ϑdϑ∫0q​r3dr=4πq4​.
(10)
Consequently
∫V​y2dV=4πC4​∫0H​(1−H2z2​)2dz=152π​C4H.
(11)
The outward unit normal vector on D is −ez​, so its flux is −2πC2. Applying the divergence theorem to the closed surface and subtracting this disk contribution gives
∫S​A⋅ndS=2πcosh2R+152π​cosh4RsinhR.​
(12)
This is a special case of polynomial flux through a half-ellipsoid. Including the closing disk is essential: the constant vertical component has zero divergence but nonzero flux through the open curved surface.

a OurBigBook.com
Seek a nonzero separated solution ψ=T(t)R(r)Θ(θ). Substitution into the heat equation and division by the product gives
κTT′​=r2R(r2R′)′​+r2Θsinθ1​(sinθΘ′)′.
(13)
The left side depends only on time, so set it to −k2. Multiplication by r2 then separates the angular dependence, with separation constant ℓ(ℓ+1). The three ordinary differential equations are
T′+κk2T=0,​
(14)
sinθ1​(sinθΘ′)′+ℓ(ℓ+1)Θ=0,​
(15)
(r2R′)′+[k2r2−ℓ(ℓ+1)]R=0.​
(16)
The temporal solution is T=T0​e−κk2t. With q=cosθ, the angular equation is the Legendre differential equation; regularity at both angular endpoints selects ℓ=0,1,2,… and Θ∝Pℓ​(q), the Legendre polynomial. The radial equation has the Spherical Bessel functions jℓ​(kr) and yℓ​(kr) for k>0. Regularity at r=0, if imposed, excludes the singular second solution. For k=0 the radial powers are rℓ and r−ℓ−1. Without specified radial boundary conditions, no discrete set of k is selected; −k2 is a convention for the temporal separation constant.

b OurBigBook.com
For spherical symmetry the angular mode is ℓ=0. Put u(t,r)=rψ(t,r). Direct differentiation gives
r21​(r2ψr​)r​=rurr​​,ψt​=rut​​,
(17)
so the radial heat equation in three dimensions becomes the ordinary one-dimensional heat equation ut​=κurr​. Since r±​>0, the zero endpoint temperatures become u(t,r±​)=0.
Write L=r+​−r−​. The two initial sine modes already satisfy these Dirichlet boundary conditions; their squared wave numbers are (π/L)2 and (2π/L)2. Each therefore evolves independently with its corresponding exponential decay. Dividing back by r gives
ψ(t,r)=r1​[e−κπ2t/L2sinLπ(r+​−r)​+e−4κπ2t/L2sinL2π(r+​−r)​].​
(18)
At t=0 the initial profile is recovered, and each sine is zero at both endpoints. The first mode decays four times more slowly in its exponential rate than the second. This is the two-mode instance of the spherical-shell heat equation via radial rescaling; uniqueness follows, for example, by applying the heat equation energy identity to the difference of two solutions.

a OurBigBook.com
For a fixed source point ξ∈(a,b), the Green function is defined by
Lx​G(x;ξ)=δ(x−ξ),G(a;ξ)=G(b;ξ)=0,​
(19)
where δ is the Dirac delta distribution and the operator acts on x. The corresponding solution is
y(x)=∫ab​G(x;ξ)f(ξ)dξ.​
(20)
Applying Lx​ under the integral gives f(x) by the defining delta identity, while the endpoint values vanish. With the stated continuous coefficients, one may define the normalized distributional equation Gxx​+(β/α)Gx​+(γ/α)G=δ(x−ξ)/α(ξ); this avoids multiplying a general distributional second derivative by a merely continuous coefficient.
Existence of this inverse Green function additionally requires that the homogeneous two-point boundary value problem have only the zero solution. The assumptions printed in the question alone do not ensure this: y′′+y on [0,π] has the nonzero zero-endpoint solution sinx. At such resonance there are solvability conditions and no ordinary inverse kernel for arbitrary f. The construction below is nonresonant.

Solution
Words: 72
i OurBigBook.com
Suppose the piecewise smooth Green function has jump [G]ξ​=G(ξ+;ξ)−G(ξ−;ξ). Its first distributional derivative then contains [G]ξ​δ(x−ξ), and its second contains [G]ξ​δ′(x−ξ). In the normalized equation from part (a), the first-derivative term can supply a delta but no delta derivative. The right side has only a delta. Thus its delta-derivative coefficient must vanish:
[G]ξ​=0.​
(21)
Equivalently, the two homogeneous branches must join continuously. This is the continuity part of the jump condition for a second-order Green function.

ii

ii OurBigBook.com
Now G is continuous, so Gx​ has no delta contribution. Integrate its normalized differential equation over (ξ−ϵ,ξ+ϵ). The bounded lower-order terms have integrals tending to zero, while the integral of Gxx​ is the difference of the two one-sided first derivatives. Hence the jump condition is
Gx​(ξ+;ξ)−Gx​(ξ−;ξ)=α(ξ)1​.​
(22)
The denominator is evaluated at the source point; it is not a variable x left over after taking the limits. The positivity or negativity of this jump follows the sign convention used for the leading coefficient of L.

The homogeneous characteristic equation is r2−2r+2=0, with roots 1±i. Choose the endpoint-adapted homogeneous solutions
u(x)=exsinx,v(x)=excosx,
(23)
so that u(0)=0 and v(π/2)=0. Their Wronskian is
W(x)=u(x)v′(x)−u′(x)v(x)=−e2x,
(24)
which never vanishes. A continuous Green function with the required endpoints has the form C(ξ)u(x<​)v(x>​), where x<​=min(x,ξ) and x>​=max(x,ξ). Its derivative jump is C(ξ)W(ξ). Because the leading coefficient is one, part (b) requires this to equal one. Therefore
G(x;ξ)=−ex−ξsinx<​cosx>​.​
(25)
In particular, the branches are −ex−ξsinxcosξ for x≤ξ and −ex−ξsinξcosx for x≥ξ. This is the Dirichlet Green function for a conjugated harmonic oscillator with interval length π/2, drift parameter one and oscillator wave number one.

Insert the source into the Green-function representation and split the integral at its source discontinuity in derivative:
y(x)​=−excosx∫0x​sinξdξ−exsinx∫xπ/2​cosξdξ=−ex[cosx(1−cosx)+sinx(1−sinx)].​

y(x)=ex(1−cosx−sinx).​

a OurBigBook.com
First take a Schwartz function, so that Fourier inversion and the exchange of integrals are justified. Inserting the inverse transform of the complex conjugate gives
∫R​∣f(x)∣2dx​=2π1​∫R​∫R​f(x)f​(k)​e−ikxdkdx=2π1​∫R​f​(k)​[∫R​f(x)e−ikxdx]dk=2π1​∫R​∣f​(k)∣2dk.​​
(28)
For f∈L1∩L2, approximate it by Schwartz functions in both norms. The identity just proved makes their transforms a Cauchy sequence in L2 space, while convergence in L1 space makes the transforms converge uniformly to the defining transform of f. Thus the two transform limits agree, and passing to the L2 norms proves the finite Parseval identity. This is the normalization of the Plancherel theorem appropriate to the paper.
There is a qualification to the printed hypothesis: absolute integrability alone does not guarantee a finite square integral. For instance f(x)=x−3/4 on (0,1) and zero elsewhere belongs to L1 but not L2. For an L1 function of this kind the transform is not in L2 either, by L2 density from a square-integrable Fourier transform, so both sides are infinite if the identity is interpreted in that extended sense. The finite equality requires square integrability as well.

Use the trigonometric identity 2cos2(ax)=1+cos(2ax) and express the cosine as a sum of two complex exponentials. The Fourier transform of each exponential is a shifted Dirac delta distribution:
F[1]=2πδ(k),F[e±2iax]=2πδ(k∓2a).
(29)
By linearity,
f​(k)=2πδ(k)+πδ(k−2a)+πδ(k+2a).​
(30)
The original function does not decay and is not absolutely integrable on the real line, so this answer is a tempered distribution, rather than an ordinary convergent Fourier integral. Its three lines represent the constant part and the two opposite spatial frequencies.

Solution

Words: 154
c OurBigBook.com
The input is even, so its Fourier transform is real and even. Decomposing the cosine into complex exponentials and integrating over its support gives
f​(k)=k−1sin[(k−1)a]​+k+1sin[(k+1)a]​.
(31)
Combining the fractions and using the angle addition formula yields
f​(k)=k2−12kcosasin(ak)−2sinacos(ak)​,λ=2,μ=−2.​
(32)
The apparent poles at k=±1 are removable singularities; either the integral or the sine-quotient limit gives f​(±1)=a+sin(2a)/2.
If cosa=0, expansion of the denominator gives
f​(k)=k2cosasin(ak)​−k22sinacos(ak)​+O(∣k∣−3).
(33)
The oscillatory envelope is therefore O(∣k∣−1). At a=π/2+nπ, n=0,1,2,…, the endpoint values vanish and the first term cancels:
cosa=0:f​(k)=−k22sinacos(ak)​+O(∣k∣−4).​
(34)
This gives an O(∣k∣−2) envelope. At general a the truncation creates jumps in the function; at these special values it leaves the function continuous but creates jumps in its first derivative. Each additional degree of endpoint smoothness gives another inverse power, as explained by Fourier decay from a derivative jump. The exact example is the Fourier transform of a truncated cosine; isolated zeros of its oscillatory factors do not change the envelope order.

The columns of Rz​ are an orthonormal basis, since cos2ϕ+sin2ϕ=1 and the first two columns have zero dot product. Thus RzT​Rz​=I: it is an orthogonal matrix. Consequently
∣v′∣2=(Rz​v)T(Rz​v)=vTRzT​Rz​v=vTv,
(35)
and hence ∣v′∣=∣v∣​. This is the preservation of the Euclidean norm by a rotation matrix.

b

Words: 120 Articles: 1
5 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 120
b OurBigBook.com
The z direction is fixed, giving the eigenvalue one. The planar block has characteristic polynomial
(cosϕ−λ)2+sin2ϕ=λ2−2λcosϕ+1.
(36)
Thus the full list of eigenvalues is
1,eiϕ,e−iϕ.​
(37)
The last two are real precisely when sinϕ=0, so all three are real exactly for ϕ∈πZ​. At even multiples of π the matrix is the identity and every vector is fixed. At odd multiples it is a half-turn: the axial eigenvalue remains +1, while the whole perpendicular plane has eigenvalue −1.
For other angles, the only real eigenvector direction is the rotation axis; the perpendicular plane is rotated rather than preserving an individual real direction. Its complex eigenvectors can be taken as (1,−i,0)T and (1,i,0)T for eiϕ and e−iϕ, respectively. These represent the two complex conjugate planar eigenvalues.

A product of orthogonal matrices is orthogonal. In fact,
R1T​R1​=RyT​RzT​Rz​Ry​=RyT​Ry​=I.
(39)
Thus R1​ is orthogonal for every θ,ϕ.​ Its determinant is also one, since each factor has determinant one, so it remains a proper rotation matrix.

ii OurBigBook.com
Both factors and their product are real, so the Hermitian conjugate equals the transpose. Part (i) therefore gives
R1†​R1​=R1T​R1​=I.
(40)
Hence R1​ is unitary for every θ,ϕ.​ A real orthogonal matrix is always a unitary matrix.

iii

Words: 92 Articles: 1
d OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 92
iii OurBigBook.com
A real matrix is a Hermitian matrix exactly when it is a symmetric matrix. Since R1​ is orthogonal, this is equivalent to R1​=R1−1​, or R12​=I. A generic rotation does not satisfy this; for example θ=0, ϕ=π/2 gives a nonsymmetric quarter-turn. Thus R1​ is not Hermitian in general.​
The exceptions are the identity and half-turns, as characterized by real rotation matrices that are Hermitian. For this product, a half-turn occurs when either θ or ϕ is an odd multiple of π; the identity occurs when both are even multiples. For example, the half-turn condition follows from trR1​=(1+cosθ)(1+cosϕ)−1=−1.

The Hermitian conjugate of a real matrix is its transpose, so
M†=(R1​−R1T​)T=R1T​−R1​=−M.
(41)
Therefore M is anti-Hermitian for all θ,ϕ.​ It is also a real skew-symmetric matrix. It is Hermitian as well only in the exceptional case M=0, precisely when R1​ is symmetric. This includes the identity and half-turn cases from part (d), so the zero-matrix overlap should not be excluded.

Let A=A† be a Hermitian matrix and Av=λv with v=0. The scalar v†Av equals its own complex conjugate, because
(v†Av)∗=v†A†v=v†Av.
(47)
Since v†Av=λv†v and the squared norm v†v is positive, λ∈R​.
Now take Au=λu and Av=μv. The inner product satisfies
u†Av=μu†v,u†Av=(Au)†v=λu†v=λu†v.
(48)
Subtracting gives (μ−λ)u†v=0. Thus distinct eigenvalues imply u†v=0​, proving orthogonality of the corresponding eigenvectors. Within a degenerate eigenspace, an orthonormal basis may be chosen, but arbitrary distinct vectors in that same eigenspace need not be orthogonal.

v†v=(Uv)†(Uv)=∣μ∣2v†v.

Division by the positive squared norm gives ∣μ∣=1​. Thus every eigenvalue lies on the unit circle.

Part (a) makes each λj​ real. In the eigenvector basis,
(A+iaI)ej​=(λj​+ia)ej​,
(50)
and ∣λj​+ia∣2=λj2​+a2>0. Hence A+iaI is invertible​.
All factors that are rational functions of A commute. Taking the Hermitian conjugate reverses product order and gives
V†=(A−iaI)−1(A+iaI).
(51)
Therefore
V†V=(A−iaI)−1(A+iaI)(A−iaI)(A+iaI)−1=I,
(52)
so V is unitary​. This is a Cayley transform of a Hermitian matrix, with scale a and the convention that an infinite real eigenvalue maps to one.
Applying it to each eigenvector yields
Vej​=νj​ej​,νj​=λj​+iaλj​−ia​.​
(53)
The eigenvectors are unchanged, and ∣νj​∣=1 because numerator and denominator are complex conjugates. No νj​ equals one when a>0. The scalar map is injective on real λ, so the eigenspaces, including any degeneracies, are preserved exactly.

B†=−i(I−U−1)−1(I+U−1).
(54)
The factorization I−U−1=−U−1(I−U) gives (I−U−1)−1=−(I−U)−1U, while I+U−1=U−1(I+U). Consequently
B†=i(I−U)−1(I+U)=i(I+U)(I−U)−1=B​.
(55)
The last equality uses the fact that I+U commutes with I−U and its inverse. Thus B is a Hermitian matrix. The exclusion of the eigenvalue one is essential to define the inverse. Spectrally, an eigenvalue eiϑ=1 is sent to −cot(ϑ/2), a real number. This is the inverse Cayley transform of a unitary matrix without eigenvalue one.

Using the exponential form of the complex cosine, cosz=0 is equivalent to e2iz=−1. Thus the zeros are exactly
zn​=2π​+nπ,n∈Z.​
(61)
At each point cos′(zn​)=−sinzn​=0, so the cosine has a simple zero. Cubing it gives
cos3z=[−sinzn​]3(z−zn​)3+O((z−zn​)4).
(62)
The order of a zero of a holomorphic function is therefore three at every zero. There are no finite singularities because this is an entire function.
To classify infinity, examine cos3(1/w) at w=0. The identity cos3z=(3cosz+cos3z)/4 shows that its Laurent series contains the nonzero negative-power coefficients
4(2m)!(−1)m(3+32m)​w−2m,m≥1.
(63)
There are infinitely many terms in the principal part, the criterion for an essential singularity. Therefore ∞ is an essential singularity, not a pole.​ This is also the general characterization of a nonpolynomial entire function at infinity.

After division by the leading coefficient, write y′′+P(x)y′+Q(x)y=0, where
P(x)=−x(1+x)1​,Q(x)=4x2(1+x)x+3​.
(68)
The only finite singular points of a differential equation are x=0 and x=−1​. At zero, xP=−1/(1+x) and x2Q=(x+3)/[4(1+x)] are analytic. At −1, (x+1)P=−1/x and (x+1)2Q=(x+1)(x+3)/(4x2) are analytic. The regular singular point criterion for a second-order equation therefore makes both points regular.
If infinity is included, it is a regular singular point at infinity as well: P(x)=O(x−2) and Q(x)=1/(4x2)+O(x−3). Equivalently, with t=1/x the transformed coefficients are P=2/t+1/(1+t) and Q​=(1+3t)/[4t2(1+t)], which satisfy the same regular-singular criterion at t=0.

For the Frobenius solution, differentiate term by term:
y′=∑n≥0​(n+σ)an​xn+σ−1,y′′=∑n≥0​(n+σ)(n+σ−1)an​xn+σ−2.
(69)
The unshifted terms in the equation have coefficient [4(n+σ)(n+σ−1)−4(n+σ)+3]an​. The extra factors of x give the shifted contribution [4(n+σ)(n+σ−1)+1]an​xn+σ+1. Equating the coefficient of xk+σ for k≥1 gives the linear recurrence relation
[4(k+σ)2−8(k+σ)+3]ak​+[4(k+σ−1)(k+σ−2)+1]ak−1​=0.​
(70)
Factoring both coefficients is especially useful:
(2k+2σ−3)[(2k+2σ−1)ak​+(2k+2σ−3)ak−1​]=0.​
(71)
The separate lowest-power equation is (4σ2−8σ+3)a0​=0. Do not cancel 2k+2σ−3 when it vanishes: that is the possible undetermined coefficient at Frobenius resonance.

On the cylindrical surface r=R, the line element is ds2=R2dθ2+dz2. For a single-valued path parametrized by increasing θ,
L[z]=∫θ1​θ2​​R2+z′2​dθ.​
(85)
The integrand has no explicit z, so its Euler-Lagrange equation gives the constant conjugate quantity z′/R2+z′2​. Its derivative with respect to z′ is strictly positive, hence z′ itself is constant. The two endpoints determine
z(θ)=z1​+πz2​−z1​​(θ+2π​),−2π​≤θ≤2π​.​
(86)
This is a constant-pitch helix on the cylinder. To verify global minimality, unroll the cylinder with planar coordinates (Rθ,z). The path becomes a straight line between points separated by πR and z2​−z1​, so the triangle inequality for arc length gives
Lmin​=π2R2+(z2​−z1​)2​.​
(87)
This is the standard description of geodesics on a circular cylinder.

Solution
Words: 206
ii OurBigBook.com
The downward drop from the starting rim to angle θ is Rcosθ. With no dissipative forces, conservation of energy gives mv2/2=mgRcosθ, so v=2gRcosθ​. Dividing the line element by this speed yields
T[z]=2gR​1​∫−π/2π/2​cosθR2+z′2​​dθ.​
(88)
The endpoint singularities are integrable for the minimizing path. The integrand is independent of z; its Euler-Lagrange equation gives a constant K, after absorbing the overall prefactor:
cosθ​R2+z′2​z′​=K.
(89)
Solving for z′ and taking the positive branch required by z2​>z1​ gives
dθdz​=1−K2cosθ​RKcosθ​​,0<K<1.​
(90)
The constant is fixed implicitly by
z2​−z1​=RK∫−π/2π/2​1−K2cosθ​cosθ​​dθ.
(91)
This integral is strictly increasing from zero to infinity as K increases from zero to one, so every finite positive separation selects a unique K. The time integrand has second derivative R2/[cosθ​(R2+z′2)3/2]>0 with respect to z′. Its supporting-line inequality, integrated between fixed endpoints with constant first derivative with respect to z′, proves this stationary path is the unique global minimum within the stated single-valued class.
As θ↓−π/2, z′→0. Therefore the skater should initially head directly down the curved ramp, perpendicular to the cylinder axis, and gain axial motion later. The path differs from the constant-pitch shortest route because extra distance is cheaper in time near the faster, lower part of the ramp. This is the brachistochrone on a horizontal half-cylinder.

Ly=−ay′′−(a′+b)y′−cy,Ly=−awy′′−(aw)′y′−wcy.
(92)
Equality L=wL requires a=a, c=c, and (aw)′=w(a′+b). Thus aw′=bw, giving the positive integrating factor
a=a,c=c,w(x)=Cexp[∫x0​x​a(s)b(s)​ds],C>0.​
(93)
With p=aw>0, the result is the Sturm-Liouville form L=−(pd/dx)′−wc. The arbitrary positive multiplier C rescales both sides of the eigenvalue problem and does not change its eigenvalues. The coefficient a′ is already present in the divergence term of L; it must not be counted a second time in the exponential.

Fix one self-adjoint choice of separated homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions or Neumann boundary conditions at each endpoint. The stated product condition then makes the boundary term [awyy′]αβ​ vanish. Multiplication of Ly=λwy by y and integration by parts give
λ∫αβ​wy2dx=∫αβ​yLydx=∫αβ​[aw(y′)2−wcy2]dx.
(94)
Hence define the quadratic functionals
F[y]=∫αβ​yLydx=∫αβ​[aw(y′)2−wcy2]dx,G[y]=∫αβ​wy2dx,​
(95)
and Λ[y]=F[y]/G[y] for nonzero admissible y. The first expression for F is linear in the operator L, and G is linear in the weight w.
To prove the minimum statement, expand an admissible function in a complete weighted orthonormal system of eigenfunctions of the Sturm-Liouville problem, y=∑n​cn​yn​, with ordered eigenvalues λ0​≤λ1​≤⋯. Self-adjointness and orthogonality of Sturm-Liouville eigenfunctions give
Λ[y]=∑n​cn2​∑n​λn​cn2​​≥λ0​.
(96)
Equality is attained by a lowest eigenfunction, so
λmin​=y=0min​Λ[y].​
(97)
This is the Rayleigh-Ritz variational principle. The endpoint product condition is shorthand for fixed choices of boundary type: allowing each trial function to choose different endpoint types would not define one fixed self-adjoint eigenvalue problem.

−dxd​[(1+x)e2xy′]=λe2xy,y(0)=0,y′(1)=0.​

The trial y=xe−x is admissible because y(0)=0 and y′=e−x(1−x) vanishes at one. Its Rayleigh quotient has numerator
F[y]=∫01​(1+x)(1−x)2dx=∫01​(1−x−x2+x3)dx=125​

and denominator
G[y]=∫01​x2dx=31​.
(100)
Consequently the Rayleigh-Ritz variational principle gives
λmin​≤45​.​
(101)
The numerator is positive for every nonzero admissible function, so the lowest eigenvalue is positive. The trial is not an exact eigenfunction: substituting it would require x2+2x−1=λx for every x. Thus the upper inequality is actually strict. This example underlies the exponential-polynomial trial space for a mixed Sturm-Liouville problem.

i OurBigBook.com
For the added trial term qn​=xne−Ax, the left Dirichlet boundary condition is automatic for a positive integer n. At the right endpoint,
qn′​(1)=e−A(n−A).
(102)
To preserve y′(1)=0 for an arbitrary variational coefficient C, choose A=n​. Then minimize the Rayleigh quotient of xe−x+Cxne−nx over C.
Since C=0 remains available, this optimization cannot worsen the original upper bound. For n=1, the added function is a multiple of the first trial, so the quotient does not change: an independent choice n≥2 is needed for extra freedom. More generally, several such functions form the exponential-polynomial trial space for a mixed Sturm-Liouville problem, and the Rayleigh-Ritz method reduces minimization to a small generalized eigenvalue problem.

The added sine vanishes at zero. Its derivative at one is BcosB, so nontrivial admissible choices are
B=(m+21​)π,m=0,1,2,….​
(103)
Negative values give the same trial directions after changing the sign of C; B=0 adds nothing. For each choice, minimize the Rayleigh quotient of xe−x+Csin(Bx) over C, or optimize over several coefficients simultaneously. The original trial is included, so the best bound is no larger than 5/4. Enlarging the trial subspace successively is the Rayleigh-Ritz method; the boundary-compatible half-integer sines provide additional independent shapes.
